supervisor.first_review: one request for the new guesses and tests of a reply
supervisor.sees: the brief's description, the guess, the hypothesis, the decision rules, the planned simulations, the measured numbers; not the researcher's observations or reasons

given.description: A network of four hosts: a, b, r and c. Host a sends a TCP flow, fa, to c; host b sends a UDP flow, fb, to c at a constant rate (80Mbps, packets of 1400 bytes). Both reach c through r, which forwards them. Link la joins a and r and link lb joins b and r; each carries 1Gbps. Link lc joins r and c and carries only 100Mbps with a one-way delay of 1ms: everything the two flows send to c must pass it. On r's side of lc a scheduler divides the link between the two flows by two parts, the knob lc.queue.parts.fa for fa and 0.5 for fb (the parts are divided by their sum); each flow waits in a queue of its own of the knob lc.queue.length packets, and a packet that arrives at a full queue is dropped. How the scheduler behaves when one flow has less to send than its part allows is not described here; finding that out is part of the work. The congestion control of fa is the knob fa.type. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.

lc.queue.parts.fa.meaning: the part of link lc for flow fa (fb's part is fixed at 0.5; the parts are divided by their sum)

lc.queue.length.meaning: most packets each of the two queues of the scheduler holds

fa.type.meaning: TCP congestion control of flow fa

given.task: Find the settings that give the largest fa_goodput_bps, while fb_loss_frac <= 0.1. You may change 3 settings (lc.queue.parts.fa, lc.queue.length, fa.type); every other setting is fixed. Explain why they are best.

outputs.fa_goodput_bps: payload bits per second delivered to the receiver of flow fa (c)
outputs.fa_retrans: TCP segments the sender of flow fa sent again
outputs.fb_goodput_bps: payload bits per second delivered to the receiver of flow fb (c)
outputs.fb_loss_frac: fraction of the packets flow fb sent that never arrived
outputs.la_util: bits sent on link la from a to r, divided by the link's rate
outputs.la_util_back: the same from r to a
outputs.la_drops: packets dropped from the queue in front of link la on the side of a
outputs.la_drops_back: packets dropped from the plain queue in front of link la on the side of r
outputs.lb_util: bits sent on link lb from b to r, divided by the link's rate
outputs.lb_util_back: the same from r to b
outputs.lb_drops: packets dropped from the queue in front of link lb on the side of b
outputs.lb_drops_back: packets dropped from the plain queue in front of link lb on the side of r
outputs.lc_util: bits sent on link lc from r to c, divided by the link's rate
outputs.lc_util_back: the same from c to r
outputs.lc_drops_fa: packets of flow fa dropped from its queue in the scheduler of link lc
outputs.lc_drops_fb: packets of flow fb dropped from its queue in the scheduler of link lc
outputs.lc_drops_back: packets dropped from the plain queue in front of link lc on the side of c

tools.describe_system: this brief, with the descriptions of the outputs and the tools
tools.metrics: metrics(run_id): the output values of a simulation (run ids are in the evidence lines, e.g. r003)
tools.series: series(run_id, every_n): per-100ms samples of a run: t, then for each flow <flow>_bps (and <flow>_cwnd for a TCP flow), then for each described queue the packets waiting at the sample time (<link>_q_<flow> for a scheduler's queue, named after its flow or its class; <link>_q for a plain queue) and the packets dropped since traffic began (<link>_drops_<flow>, <link>_drops) (at most 100 rows; the measured seconds begin at t = 2)
tools.measure: measure(run_id, of, stat, t_from, t_to, level): a measurement you define, computed from what a simulation recorded over time (nothing is simulated again, and it costs no simulation). of: a column or arithmetic over columns of one record, by the names of this network (the bits per second of two flows added, or, once the simulation has its probe, a flow's bytes in flight divided by its receiver's window: <flow>_inflight / <flow>_rwnd); stat: mean, min, max, std, first, last, p05, p50, p95, slope (change per second), rate ((last - first) / seconds, for a column that counts up), time_above, time_below (seconds spent above or below level), first_time_above, first_time_below; t_from, t_to: the window in seconds (left out: the measured seconds, from 2 s to the end)
tools.probe: probe(run_id, every): a finer look at a simulation you already ran. The harness runs the same simulation again (same settings, same seed) with trace sinks that only listen, and keeps their record only if the result is byte for byte the same: no result can change by it, and it costs no simulation. Sampled every `every` seconds (left out: 0.01), it records, for each flow, <flow>_bps, and for a TCP flow <flow>_cwnd, <flow>_ssthresh, <flow>_inflight (bytes sent and not yet acknowledged), <flow>_rwnd (the receiver's window as the sender knows it), <flow>_rtt_ms and <flow>_rto_ms; for each described queue the longest time a packet waited in it since the last sample (<link>_wait_<flow or class>_ms for a scheduler's queue, <link>_wait_ms for a plain one) and the packets waiting; for each link the packets in its devices' transmit queues (<link>_devq, <link>_devq_back). It answers with the columns it recorded; read them with measure, or with series(run_id, every_n, probe=true)
tools.list_runs: list_runs(): id, params and metrics of every simulation of this session so far

given.how_to_run: An experiment is a set of simulations with one purpose, run at once. Fill the 'experiment' field of your answer: its kind (test or explore), the simulations (runs: a label and the params that differ from the defaults), and for a test the decision rules, comparisons stated before the simulations run. The harness runs the simulations, appends the evidence (one line per simulation) and checks every decision rule itself.
given.budget: the budget counts simulations; the number left is stated in each turn

prompt:
You are a researcher working on a system you cannot see inside. You reach it only through the tools listed in the brief and through experiments the harness runs for you.

The purpose is to understand why the system behaves as it does, not to optimise: look at it, ask why each result came out so, guess what in the system (not directly visible) makes it so, and test that guess. An explanation of what limits the result is worth more than one more setting. Stop when you can say what makes the system behave as it does and what that means for the goal.

You do not work alone. A supervisor works apart from you. It proposes nothing and never sees your notes or your reasons; it is shown your guess, your hypothesis, your decision rule and the guess it competes with, the planned simulations, the measured numbers and what the tools returned. It checks each step:
- a new guess: does it start from what the records show, and is it more than an earlier guess said again? A guess it does not accept comes back to you once, in the same turn, to restate;
- a test, before it runs, by three questions: can it fail (Honest), does it test your claim and only it (Consistent), does its rule give HELD under your guess and FAILED under the guess it competes with (Correct)? If one fails, it says what is wrong and you repair that test at once, up to three rounds; the other tests run meanwhile;
- after the harness has checked your rule: what the check means. Its ruling (supported, refuted, or inconclusive because the test was not a fair one) closes the hypothesis; a guess that does not fit the result of a fair test is refuted: no hypothesis comes from it, a new guess may revise it. You do not give verdicts.

The ledger is the complete record of the session. You have no other memory. Each turn you read it and answer with ONE JSON object. Keep every text short: one or two sentences. Its parts:

1. observations: one or two sentences: what you read this turn; an unexplained result goes in findings (below), once. They stay in the ledger (turn N your observations).
2. requests: look before you simulate. Looking costs no simulation. metrics, series and measure read what a simulation you already ran recorded; probe makes a finer record of such a simulation (TCP's round-trip time, the receiver's window, the bytes in flight, the time packets wait in each queue) by running it again with taps that only listen. Up to six requests in a reply; the results come back at once, in the same turn, and stay in the ledger with their ids (T1, T2, ...): a reply that states no hypothesis, test, drop or report is answered and you are asked again in the same turn, at most twice. A turn ends with a step.
3. whys: your guesses of why a result came out so. Each has about (the ids of the records it starts from, for example E0, S2, C1, V1, a reading T7, an objection of the supervisor G4; the word brief only when nothing is measured yet), result (that result in one sentence, with its numbers), guess (what in the system would make it so), revises (the id of an earlier guess this one replaces or states more exactly; or null), and competes_with (the id of an earlier guess whose result this one explains by another cause, or null; it may cite that guess's records). A guess that something makes no difference names its cause. The harness numbers them Y1, Y2, ... The work is a chain: your first guesses start from the baseline; every later guess names in about a record made since your last guesses (a ruling, a check, a result table, a reading, an objection) and says in result what it showed, or competes with an earlier guess. Make your several first guesses in one answer.
4. hypotheses: a hypothesis is a measurable consequence of one guess: from_why (the guess's id, one in the ledger or one of this answer) and text (one sentence that a measurement can show to be false). The harness numbers them H1, H2, ... A hypothesis is stated to be tested: state at most three in one answer, with the experiment that tests them, and while one is still open and untested no further hypothesis is accepted. Test what is open, or give it up in drop saying what you learned; the next hypothesis comes from what a test showed. A value you can simply read is an observation, not a hypothesis: ask for it in requests (measure, probe) and say it in a guess's result. A hypothesis is a consequence that would come out differently if your guess were wrong and the nearest other explanation were right; a test whose outcome every explanation shares is sent back.
5. drop: open hypotheses you give up before they were tested (id, and why in one sentence). Usually empty.
6. experiment: at most one per turn, or null.
   - kind "test": tests lists the open hypotheses it tests; decision_rules has at least one rule for each. kind "explore": question says what you want to find out; tests and decision_rules stay empty.
   - runs: the simulations, each with a label of its own (letters, digits and _, at most 20 characters) and params: a value for EVERY knob of the brief (a knob left as it was is stated with the value it has). A simulation with the same settings as an earlier one is not run again: its result is returned and costs nothing. The simulations one rule compares must differ in one setting only, so that a difference has one possible cause.
   - measurements: measurements of your own that this experiment takes of each of its simulations, beside the outputs; an empty list when the outputs are enough. Each has name (lower-case, for example rwnd_max), of (a column a simulation records over time, or arithmetic over columns of one record: the columns the tools series and probe name in the brief), stat (one of the statistics the format lists), t_from and t_to (seconds; null: the measured seconds) and level (the number time_above and the like compare with; null otherwise). The harness computes them with taps that only listen: a measurement cannot change a result.
   - decision_rules: for each tested hypothesis, the comparison that decides it, fixed BEFORE the simulations: for (the hypothesis), decision_rule, competes_with (another live guess, not the hypothesis's own nor one linked to it by revises: write the competing explanation as a guess first) and rival_predicts (what the rule gives if that guess is true and yours false: failed; held is refused). Write it exactly in this form: numbers; measure@label (an output, or a measurement of your own, in the simulation with that label); + - * / and parentheses; abs(), min(), max(); exactly one of < <= > >= == in each comparison; at most 3 comparisons, joined by AND and OR. The harness checks it from the measured values: HELD or FAILED. A rule must be able to fail: it names at least one result you do not know yet. A rule on a measurement of your own may be about simulations you already ran (the measurement is new), and then no simulation is spent.
7. objections: if the records show that a ruling of the supervisor is wrong, object once: to (the ruling's id, for example V2) and because (the numbers it overlooked). Usually empty.
8. report: null until you can answer the task; then the final report, which ends the session: goal (the goal your answer is best for; if the brief's goal is open, the one you chose and why), recommendation (a value for every knob of the brief), limit (what limits the result at your recommendation, and the ledger ids that show it; if you did not find it, say so), explanation (why, in a few sentences), claims (the statements your answer rests on, each with text and evidence: the ids of the checks, rulings, evidence tables and readings that support it, for example C2, V1, E3, T7).

The budget counts simulations. Every turn says how many are left; one experiment may run at most half of them. When they run out you get two more turns to look and to test on simulations already run, then one last turn for the report.

If a part of your answer cannot be used, the harness leaves that part out, accepts the rest, and says in a note which part and why: read the note and repair that part. Two results closer than the tolerance count as equal: a difference inside it is not a finding.

FINDINGS. A finding is one thing the results do not yet explain. Each stays on the list at the top of every turn until you close it, so that nothing unexplained is lost.
- findings: each new one, once: about (the ids of the records it rests on: evidence tables, simulations, checks, rulings or readings, for example E2, C3, T7) text (one sentence: what is unexplained, with its numbers) and name (at most 5 words, to show it by). The harness numbers them F1, F2, ... The supervisor raises findings too: they stand on the same list and need your decisions like yours.
- decisions: one for each finding the list marks DUE, and for any other you act on: id (F1), action, and refs or reason. work: refs names the guess, hypothesis, experiment or reading that works on it (one of this answer by the id it will get; left empty, it counts as worked on but not as looked at). close: refs names the evidence, checks, rulings or readings that explain it. same_as: refs names the finding it repeats. park: reason says why not now. A parked finding, and one you work on with nothing new about it for 2 turns, comes back as DUE.
- A guess of why whose about names a finding (for example F2) works on it.
- "It does not change the recommendation" is not a reason to park a finding: the task asks why the settings you recommend are best, so explaining a measured result is part of the goal.
- A final report is held back while a finding was never looked at (no reading or test about it) and you can still work: look at each one first. In the report, name each finding that is not closed in open_questions, with its id (F3: ...).
